significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish a form-(iii) predictive coupling—“robustness correlates with our mechanistic depth metric”—together with the causal result that redistributing safety effects beyond positions 1–5 increases resistance to prefilling and mid-sequence injection. This would establish both a behavioral phenomenon (early-token concentration predicts brittle refusal) and a partial mechanism (position-dependent aligned/base divergence and refusal-direction attribution), constraining which models and training changes should be robust rather than merely showing that a refusal direction exists; this targets the same load-bearing shallow-alignment issue identified by Qi et al. (2024), while Arditi et al. (2024) illustrates why locating refusal signals alone would be insufficient. The claim is determinate, and a negative result—no sharp early concentration, no robustness correlation, or no benefit from deepening—would reject alignment depth as the proposed common explanation and training target, although it would not explain the attacks instead. In the topic-substitution check, generic “mechanistic LLM safety” would not earn this score; the measurable depth–robustness law and causal redistribution are the claim-specific reasons it exceeds the topic median.

reach.justification: The named handle is a “mechanistic definition and metric of alignment depth that predicts robustness,” supplemented by a “depth-aware objective” that treats the metric as a training target. It is ex ante because the depth profile can screen an aligned model or training checkpoint before deployment or full attack evaluation, leaving an action window to retrain, and its downstream users include safety auditors and alignment-training engineers rather than only researchers explaining completed failures. After per-model re-extraction, the asserted relation still predicts that sharper concentration yields greater prefill/injection brittleness and a flatter profile yields greater robustness, although its stated reach is mainly refusal-based text safety and may vary across “RLHF vs DPO” rather than extending to unrelated safety failures or modalities. The topic-substitution check lowers no credit here: the transferable predictor and design target, not the general importance of LLM safety, support the above-median reach.
